title: Nehemiah 12:1–11
context: This list names the chiefs of the priests and the Levites who went up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua at the first return, and then traces the high-priestly line from Jeshua to Jaddua. Several names match or resemble the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:2–8 and the families listed for Joiakim’s day in 12:12–21, with differences in spelling and in which names appear. Both traditions read the list as shared ground on God’s faithfulness in preserving worship through the generations after the exile.

verses.text: Now these are the priests and the Levites who went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra,
verses.arminianNotes:
The list begins with “the priests and the Levites who went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua” (cf. Ezra 2:2; 3:2). Arminian readers note that the record connects the community of Nehemiah’s day with the first return.

The Ezra named here is usually distinguished from Ezra the scribe, who came later.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see continuity between the first returnees and the later community.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the list honors those who served at a fragile beginning, and the names root later worship in a real history.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Amariah, Malluch, Hattush.” Arminian readers note that these priestly names also appear among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:3–4.

The repetition suggests family names carried on across generations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see continuity in the priestly houses that served after the exile.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, noting that Hattush does not appear in the list for Joiakim’s day in 12:12–21.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth.” Arminian readers note that the later list in 12:14–15 has Shebaniah, Harim, and Meraioth at about these points.

Whether these are spelling differences or different names is discussed and left open here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the differences between the two lists and do not harmonize them.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the lists preserve the priestly houses, even where the forms of names vary.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah.” Arminian readers note that 12:16 has Ginnethon and Nehemiah 10:6 also has Ginnethon.

Iddo’s line includes Zechariah (12:16), often identified with the prophet of that name (cf. Zech 1:1; Ezra 5:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the identification of Iddo’s descendant Zechariah with the prophet as a common reading.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: prophets and priests together served the restored community.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Mijamin, Maadiah, Bilgah.” Arminian readers note that 12:17–18 has Miniamin, Moadiah, and Bilgah, with small differences in form.

The priestly divisions recall those set out in 1 Chronicles 24.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the priestly houses maintained after the exile.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: worship continued through ordered families of priests, as David had arranged.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah.” Arminian readers note that Jedaiah also heads a priestly family in the return lists of Ezra 2:36 and Nehemiah 7:39.

Those lists name only four priestly families and give their numbers instead of the names of chiefs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the return lists and this list record different kinds of information.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the lists side by side without harmonizing.

verses.text: Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the chiefs of the priests and of their brothers in the days of Jeshua.
verses.arminianNotes:
“These were the chiefs of the priests and of their brothers in the days of Jeshua.” Arminian readers note that the list closes by dating these leaders to the time of the first high priest after the return.

Jedaiah appears twice in the list, as also in 12:19 and 12:21.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the list framing a generation of faithful service.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the record honors “their brothers” as well as the chiefs, recognizing the many who served.

verses.text: Moreover the Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who was over the thanksgiving songs, he and his brothers.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites include Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, and Mattaniah, “who was over the thanksgiving songs, he and his brothers.” Arminian readers note the place of praise in the Levites’ work (cf. 11:17).

Jeshua and Kadmiel also head the Levites in Ezra 2:40.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see thanksgiving as a central part of the restored worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: song and gratitude belong to the service of God’s house.

verses.text: Also Bakbukiah and Unno, their brothers, were close to them according to their offices.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Also Bakbukiah and Unno, their brothers, were close to them according to their offices.” Arminian readers note that singers served together, each in an assigned place.

The arrangement may reflect antiphonal singing (cf. 12:24).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see order and partnership among those who led worship.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: different people served side by side, each according to an office.

verses.text: Jeshua became the father of Joiakim, and Joiakim became the father of Eliashib, and Eliashib became the father of Joiada,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jeshua became the father of Joiakim, and Joiakim became the father of Eliashib, and Eliashib became the father of Joiada.” Arminian readers note the line of high priests from the return onward.

Eliashib is the high priest of Nehemiah’s day (3:1; 13:28).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see continuity in the high priesthood across generations.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both note that this line reappears in the sober events of 13:28.

verses.text: and Joiada became the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan became the father of Jaddua.
verses.arminianNotes:
The line continues, “and Joiada became the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan became the father of Jaddua.” Arminian readers note that the line extends beyond Nehemiah’s time.

12:22–23 names Johanan in this place; whether Jonathan and Johanan are the same person is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the question and leave it open.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the list shows the priesthood continuing after Nehemiah, and its dating questions are left to interpreters.
